title: How we made the correct way the easy way in Amplitude
body_markdown:
# How we built golden paths for Amplitude


Amplitude is one of the most powerful tools we have at Photoroom. It is also one of the most complex.


About 95 people use Amplitude every week at Photoroom: engineers, PMs, marketers, data analysts. None of them has hours to learn it. And the rules that make the data correct, like how to name an event or which metric decides a test, are many and depend on the task. No page can hold all of them, at the moment each person needs them. And Amplitude ships new features so fast that internal documentation about it cannot stay up to date.


In[our article about the event governance Slack bot](https://www.photoroom.com/inside-photoroom/amplitude-event-governance-slack-bot-and-ai) , we said we wanted a golden path. This article explains the idea and how we applied it to Amplitude with Claude skills. Several articles will follow to go deeper: on how we create events together in Slack, how we review experiment setups etc…


## 1. The problem: one tool, many jobs


At Photoroom, Amplitude is not only a place to look at charts. It does many jobs:


-


**Tracking:** User clicks, product analytics (retention, funnels), subscription events from RevenueCat and Stripe, anomaly detection with automated reports in Slack.


-


**A/B testing:** Experiments, feature flags, and their analyses.


-


**Production control:** Feature flags read by the apps and the backends: rollouts, and which plan gives access to a feature.


-


**Cost monitoring:** AI generation credits consumed, with a unit cost per model, as a proxy for cost.


-


**User discovery:** Session replay (sampled).


-


**Shared database:** we receive all of our Amplitude events in a Snowflake database, everyday.


This is the key point: **the same events feed most of these jobs** . If an event is renamed, sent twice, or loses a property, it is not only a wrong chart. It can be a false alert in Slack, a wrong A/B test metric, a wrong cost signal, or a wrong table in our warehouse. One bad event, several broken uses.


Each job also has its own rules: naming, sources, guardrail metrics, statistics. The UI does not explain these rules. And a page cannot bring them to you: it waits to be read, and nobody reads it in the middle of a task.


## 2. What is a golden path?


A golden path is a road where **the easiest way is also the correct way** . It is never mandatory. You can always take another road, but the golden path is the one we recommend and support: the preferred way.


The term was[popularized by Spotify](https://engineering.atspotify.com/2020/8/how-we-use-golden-paths-to-solve-fragmentation-in-our-software-ecosystem) and is now a core idea in platform engineering. You do not write a long guide and hope people read it. You build a road that people want to take, because it is faster than the alternatives. The conventions are built into the road: taking it means following them without thinking about it.


Guardrails are different. A guardrail stops you when you do something wrong. For us, the guardrails are a protected main branch and a review on every branch. **The path is optional, but the guardrails are not.** We need both, but the path comes first: if the correct way takes less time than going around the process, people take the correct way.


For Amplitude, a golden path means this: you tell Claude what you want in plain language, or you give it your Notion spec. The skill asks the right questions, applies our conventions, and gives you a result that is ready for review.


## 3. Four paths: track, analyze, test, decide


Today we have 8 Amplitude skills in our[skills marketplace](https://www.photoroom.com/inside-photoroom/how-we-built-a-skills-marketplace-for-claude) . You do not need to know their names: Claude finds the right one from your request. They cover four moments.


Path


You say


The skills do


**Track**


"Here is my Notion spec, create my events"


Create your events with our conventions, on a branch, ready for review


**Analyze**


"How many users exported a video last week?" or "Compare retention in September and October"


Query Amplitude with our analysis method


**Test**


"Create my experiment" or "Check the setup of my A/B test"


Create your experiment with our defaults, and check its setup before launch


**Decide**


"Analyze my experiment"


Read the results with our statistical method, and give a recommendation


The analyze path is our most used skill. It is also under the two experiment paths: every query that a skill sends to Amplitude follows the same method.


You do not need to know where the button is in the UI. You do not need to remember that property names use Proper Case. The skill knows. If something is not clear, it asks you one precise question instead of guessing.


**Does it work?** The next articles show it, path by path, with the numbers.


## 4. Why skills, and not only the Amplitude MCP


In Amplitude, the list of events and properties, called the tracking plan, is versioned like code. You make your changes on a branch, someone reviews them, and then they are merged into main, the tracking plan that everyone uses. At Photoroom, every change goes through a branch, so nothing reaches main without a review.


When we started, the Amplitude MCP could create neither a branch nor an event. An agent could not propose a change for review. So we built the path ourselves, step by step.


-


**January 2026.** A strict event naming convention, a Notion form and a manual review.


-


**March 2026.** A Slack bot validates event names, with browser automation to create branches ([article](https://www.photoroom.com/inside-photoroom/amplitude-event-governance-slack-bot-and-ai) ).


-


**May 2026.** Claude skills create the branch, the events and their descriptions.


-


**5 June 2026.** Amplitude releases branch and create tools in its MCP.


-


**June to July 2026.** Experiment analysis, then the experiment setup check.


-


**September 2026.** Tracking plan design and the Amplitude analysis method.


-


**October 2026.** Claude in Slack reviews each new branch with the same skill, and experiment creation joins the test path.


Now the MCP can create branches and events too. Does it make our skills useless? No. **The MCP gives the hands while the skill gives the knowledge.**


The MCP knows *how* to create an event. It does not know what is correct at Photoroom: our approved list of objects, our rule that every event has a source, our default Bonferroni correction for experiments. We had a clear proof of this: when no branch was given, the MCP wrote events directly to main. Capable, but not opinionated. Main is now protected, and our skills always work on a branch.


Our most used skill shows this best. The analysis method creates nothing. It only guides the MCP: which events to trust, how to compare two periods, what a correct answer looks like at Photoroom.


Our skills also cover what the MCP does not do at all. Amplitude does not check a test setup against our rules before launch. We also keep a list of what we still miss in the MCP, and we share it with the Amplitude team.


## 5. Less dependence


Golden paths also reduce three kinds of dependence.


-


**On the UI:** Nobody needs hours of training to create an event or read a test.


-


**On people:** Before, each event waited for an approval from the data team. When one person was out of office, requests waited. Now the skill drives you, and the data team only reviews the branch.


-


**On the tool:** Our conventions live in the skills, not in Amplitude and not in one head. If Amplitude changes its UI or its MCP, or if one day we change tool, the knowledge stays. Only the calls to the tool change. The rules stay. This is also why skills age better than a page: when Amplitude ships a new feature, the MCP follows it, and our rules stay the same.


## 6. Limits


-


**A skill is only as good as its rules.** When the skill is wrong, someone must say it. We need that feedback to improve it.


-


**The review is still human.** The path makes the review fast. It does not make it optional. One day, we could have a CI that could prevent having any human in the loop if it passes.


## 7. What we learned


-


**Do not wait for the perfect tool.** A Slack bot and a skill were enough to start. When the MCP improved, we kept the knowledge and changed only the calls.


-


**Put the knowledge where the work happens.** People do not open a wiki before they create an event. They open Claude.


-


**Ask, do not guess.** For ambiguous rules, one precise question is better than a hard block. We spent a lot of time investigating how Amplitude experiments calculation work for instance. We never gave up and asked as many questions as we needed to be able to make things more clear. Luckily, the Amplitude team is always here to help.


-


**Every mistake is a candidate rule.** When we find a new mistake, we add a rule to the skill, so the next person cannot make it. This includes the mistakes of the skill itself. We are also working on an escalation log to track all


## 8. What comes next


In the next articles, we go deeper into two of the paths: how we create events together in Slack, and how we review the setup of an experiment before launch.


Amplitude is still powerful, and still complex. But you do not need to know all of it any more. You need to know where the path starts.


Thanks for reading, you can find other articles from the Photoroom data team[here](https://www.photoroom.com/inside-photoroom/category/category-4) .
